transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, it's nice to meet you too. Well, I suppose I'm here because of what's been happening at work lately, and it's really starting to bother me. I'm a jeweler, I do a lot of custom metalwork and precious stone settings, repairs, things like that, which I've done for years. But I came in today because I've been having this awful trouble when talking to my customers. 

Someone will come in and ask me a really simple question, like, just asking when a ring repair will be ready for them to pick up. Just a basic, everyday question, right? But when I try to answer them, my answer just starts going all over the place. I'll start talking about the repair invoices, and then somehow that makes me start talking about the garden soil I need to pick up for my flower beds, and before I know it I'm going on about the mortgage papers I was sorting through on my kitchen table the night before. 

I just keep talking and I can actually see them losing me. I can see their expressions change, like they have no idea how we got from a broken clasp to my garden, and honestly, neither do I. It’s just so embarrassing because I know they just want a simple date and time, and I took some college classes in business years ago so I know how to be professional, but I just can't seem to stop my thoughts from stringing all these completely unrelated things together out loud. It just spills out of me before I can catch it.
Lately, have you been feeling unusually high or euphoric?

High? Euphoric? Oh, heavens no. No, I don't think I've felt anything even close to euphoric in... well, I honestly can't even remember. 

I mean, when I hear the word euphoric, I picture someone just bouncing off the walls with joy, you know? Like... like when my sister won a little bit of money on a scratch-off ticket a few years back and she just couldn't stop talking about it. She was so thrilled she took our whole family out to this little Italian place downtown, the one with the really good garlic knots, and she was just glowing the entire night. But me? No, definitely not. I haven't had any sort of burst of happiness or extra energy like that at all. 

If anything, I just wake up, make my coffee—usually just a simple drip, nothing fancy, though sometimes I used to use the French press if I had the time on a Sunday morning... but lately, I just stick to the basic machine because I just want to get it over with. So, no, I'm definitely not feeling high or on top of the world or anything like that. I'm really just trying to get through my workday and figure out why my brain keeps jumbling up my words when I'm standing at the counter with my customers. There's certainly no euphoria in that, let me tell you, it's honestly just incredibly frustrating.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Well, yes, actually. I mean, it's not like a whole crowd of people talking to me or anything like you see in the movies, but... yes. It usually happens when I'm at work and the shop is completely quiet. You know, those lulls in the afternoon, usually around 2:30 or 3:00, when everyone is still at their own jobs and the foot traffic just dies down completely. I'll be sitting there, maybe just sorting through some jump rings or organizing my files, and I'll hear this woman's voice. 

It's always a woman, and she just mutters my name. Just my name, but it sounds like it's coming right out of the polishing room in the back. The first few times it happened, I actually got up and walked back there, thinking maybe someone had slipped through the side door without the bell ringing, or maybe my sister had dropped by to bring me lunch and was trying to surprise me. But there's never anyone there. Just the polishing wheels and the dust collector sitting there turned off. 

And it's not just the voice, either. Sometimes, in that same quiet stretch, I'll suddenly smell burning metal. If you've ever worked with a jeweler's torch, you know exactly that smell—it's very distinct, sharp, almost acidic when the flame hits the flux. I'll smell it so strongly, so clearly, that I'll actually panic for a second. I'll drop whatever I'm doing and run over to the soldering station to make sure I didn't leave a torch on or that a valve isn't leaking. I'll check the dials, I'll check the hoses, I'll even touch the tips of the torches to see if they're warm. But they're always stone cold. Everything is off. But the smell is just so real, and the voice is so real, that I just have to go check every single time, even though part of me knows by now that I'm probably going to find an empty room. It's just so unsettling, you know? To experience something so vividly and then find out it's just... not there.
Have you had any seizures?

Seizures? Oh, no. No, I've never had a seizure. I mean, I know what they look like, of course. My neighbor, well, my old neighbor from about fifteen years ago, her name was Brenda, she had this little terrier mix that used to have seizures. Poor thing would just fall over in the yard and shake, and Brenda would get so upset, naturally. She'd have to sit there on the grass with him until it passed. But me? No, nothing like that. 

I've always been pretty healthy in that regard. I mean, working with my hands all day, doing such fine, detailed work with the stones and the metal, you really need a steady hand. If I were having seizures, or even just tremors, I don't think I could do my job at all. Setting a tiny diamond into a prong setting takes so much precision, you know? You have to hold the piece just right, apply just the right amount of pressure with the tools. So, no, definitely no seizures. My hands are steady... it's just my thoughts and my words that seem to be getting all tangled up lately. But physically, no, no seizures or anything like that.
Have you been feeling unusually irritable lately?

Irritable? Well, I wouldn't say I've been unusually irritable, no. I mean, sure, everyone gets a little annoyed now and then, especially when things don't go according to plan. Like last Tuesday, I had this customer come in—a very nice lady, don't get me wrong, she's been coming to me for years—but she brought in this antique filigree ring that her grandmother had given her, and she wanted me to resize it. Now, resizing filigree is always tricky because the metal is so delicate, and if you aren't careful, you can completely ruin the pattern. So I explained all of this to her, very patiently, and told her it would take at least two weeks because I needed to order a specific type of gold solder to match the alloy perfectly. 

But then, not even three days later, she calls the shop wanting to know if it's ready! I had to explain the whole process to her all over again. And yes, in that moment, I suppose I felt a tiny bit of frustration, just because I had been so clear the first time. But I wasn't snapping at her or losing my temper. I kept my voice perfectly level and polite, just like I always do. 

And my sister, she's always telling me I have the patience of a saint, especially with the intricate work I do. You really can't be an irritable person and sit at a bench for six hours straight, peering through a loupe, trying to set a one-millimeter sapphire without scratching the surface. It requires a very calm, very centered disposition. So, no, I don't think I've been feeling unusually irritable. Just the normal, everyday little annoyances, but nothing out of the ordinary, and certainly nothing I can't handle with a deep breath and a cup of tea. It's really just the sadness and the... the confusion with my words and those strange moments in the quiet shop that are bothering me. But my temper? No, that's been perfectly fine.
Have you been feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Well, yes... yes, I have. It’s funny you phrase it like that, "most of the day, nearly every day," because that’s exactly what it feels like. It’s this constant, lingering thing. Most mornings I wake up with this flat, heavy sadness, like the color has just completely drained out of the house before I even get out of bed, let alone before I get to the shop. 

It’s hard to explain, really. You know how when you look at a beautiful piece of jewelry, maybe a really nice opal, and it has all that fire and play of color? That’s how life used to feel to me. There were bright spots, things to look forward to, even just small things like a good cup of coffee or a nice chat with a customer. But now, it’s like looking at a piece of rough, unpolished quartz. Just dull and gray. 

I’ll lie there in bed and look at the ceiling, and the thought of getting up and going through the motions just feels so... monumental. I still do it, of course, because I have the shop to run and my sister relies on me to keep things going, but the joy is just gone. I’ll sit at my bench, and even when I’m working on something I used to love, like a really intricate custom setting, I just feel this weight sitting right on my chest. It doesn't go away after lunch, it doesn't go away when I close up the shop for the evening. It’s just this quiet, heavy sadness that follows me around, day in and day out. So, yes, I would say I’ve been feeling depressed almost constantly lately. It’s exhausting, to be honest. Just exhausting to feel so empty all the time.
Have the voice and the burning-metal smell ever happened during a time when you were not feeling depressed?

Well... yes, actually. Yes, they have. It’s strange to think back on it now, because the sadness feels like it’s been here forever, but there was a time before this heavy feeling really settled in. I was actually doing quite well, keeping very busy. I was still running my evening jewelry-making classes at the community center—which I loved doing, teaching people how to solder and work with silver clay, it’s so rewarding to see their faces when they finish their first piece. And I was gardening, too. I have these beautiful heirloom tomatoes I was tending to, and some lovely climbing roses along the trellis in the back. 

But even then, when I was feeling perfectly fine, not depressed at all, I was having these... experiences. It went on for several weeks, I think. I would be in the shop, feeling completely normal, maybe just organizing my tools or sketching a new design, and I kept hearing these noises coming from the polishing room. It sounded like the tumbling machine was running, or like someone was moving the buffs around, but I was the only one there. And the smell of the burning metal would just waft in, so strong I’d have to check the torches even though I hadn't used them all day. 

And during that same time, I started getting so worried that customers were... watching the business. Not just looking in the windows, but really watching. I’d see someone pause outside the shop, maybe admiring a necklace in the display, but I’d get this overwhelming feeling that they were monitoring me, keeping track of my inventory or my hours. I even started keeping the blinds half-drawn during the day, which is terrible for a retail shop, I know, but I just couldn't shake the feeling. So, yes, all of that—the noises, the smells, the worrying—that was happening for weeks while I was still feeling quite energetic and involved with my classes and my garden, long before this terrible sadness took over.
Have you ever had a period when you needed much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?

Less sleep? No, I wouldn't say that. I've always been a fairly consistent sleeper, really. I mean, my sister always jokes that I run like clockwork, and it's true. Usually, I'm in bed by 10:30, maybe 11:00 if I've gotten caught up reading a good book—lately I've been reading this fascinating biography of René Lalique, his glasswork is just incredible, the way he incorporated those natural motifs into the Art Nouveau style, it really makes you think about how we approach design today. But anyway, yes, I'm usually asleep by 11:00 and up by 7:00, because the shop opens at 9:30 and I like to have a good hour and a half to myself in the morning to have my tea, read the paper, and just ease into the day before I have to start dealing with customers and vendors and all of that. 

Even back when I was feeling good, when I was teaching those evening classes and spending all my weekends out in the garden with the tomatoes and the roses, I still needed my full eight hours. I might have been busy and active, but I was definitely tired at the end of the day. In fact, teaching those classes takes a lot out of you, emotionally and physically, hovering over people's shoulders, making sure they don't burn themselves with the micro-torches... by the time I'd get home at 9:00 PM, I'd be ready to just collapse. So, no, I've never had a time where I was just buzzing along on three or four hours of sleep and feeling perfectly fine. If I don't get my rest, my hands get shaky, and you absolutely cannot have shaky hands when you're trying to set a tiny little diamond into a delicate prong setting. It's just not possible. So, no, I've always needed my sleep.
Was there ever a time when the voices or suspicious thoughts lasted for at least two weeks while you were not feeling depressed?

Well, yes, actually, just like I was saying earlier... it's funny how the mind works, isn't it? You kind of lose track of the timeline when you're in the thick of this heavy sadness, but yes, there was definitely a stretch of time before the depression really settled in. I was feeling quite myself, honestly. I was still running my evening classes at the community center, teaching the silver clay and the soldering, which I always found so fulfilling. And I was out in the garden every weekend, tying up those heirloom tomatoes—they get so heavy if you don't support them properly—and tending to the climbing roses. I felt perfectly fine, mood-wise. 

But even then, while I was feeling good, that's when those things started happening, and it went on for several weeks, easily. I would be in the shop, feeling completely normal, maybe sorting through a new batch of semi-precious stones that had just come in from my supplier in Jaipur—they do the most wonderful cuts on their amethysts, really top-notch work—and I'd just keep hearing these noises coming from the polishing room in the back. It was so distinct, like the tumbling machine was running or someone was shuffling the buffs around, but I was entirely alone in the store. 

And that was the exact same time I started getting so incredibly worried that people were watching the business. It wasn't just a fleeting thought, it was this persistent, gnawing worry for weeks. I'd see a customer outside, maybe just looking at the window display, and I'd be absolutely convinced they were monitoring my inventory or keeping track of when I opened and closed. I was so convinced of it that I started keeping the front blinds half-drawn during regular business hours, which my sister told me was ridiculous for a retail shop, but I just couldn't help it. So, yes, all of that—the noises from the back room, the intense worrying about being watched—that all went on for several weeks while I was still gardening and teaching, well before this awful, draining sadness took over my life.
Have you found yourself talking much less than usual lately?

Talking less? Well... I suppose it might seem like that to some people, but I don't really think so. I mean, my sister called the other day, and we were on the phone for a good forty-five minutes talking about our aunt's estate sale. It's such a complicated situation, trying to divide up all those antique furniture pieces without causing a family rift. Aunt Helen had this gorgeous Victorian settee, beautifully carved mahogany with the original horsehair stuffing, and my cousin Sarah thinks she should have it just because she has a larger living room, which is completely beside the point if you ask me. 

So, no, when I have something to say, or when I'm talking to my sister or my suppliers, I still talk just as much as I ever did. I was just on the phone with my metal supplier yesterday, actually, trying to sort out a mix-up with an order of sterling silver wire. They sent me half-round instead of dead-soft round, and you simply cannot use half-round when you're trying to do delicate wire-wrapping for pendants, it just doesn't sit right against the stones. I had to explain the whole process to the customer service representative, who clearly had no background in jewelry making whatsoever, bless his heart. I must have spent twenty minutes just trying to get him to understand the difference in the gauges and the temper of the metal. 

Now, I will say, because of this heavy, awful sadness I've been feeling, I haven't been going out to social events or chatting up the neighbors over the fence like I used to. When you feel this drained, this utterly exhausted down to your bones, the idea of making small talk about the weather or the local school board elections just feels impossible. It takes so much energy to put on a bright face and pretend everything is fine when inside you just feel like a lead weight. But as far as my actual ability to talk, or how much I speak when I do have a conversation... no, I haven't noticed any change there. I still have plenty to say, it's just that I don't always have the energy to find an audience for it right now.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

Lost interest... oh, heavens, yes. That's actually been one of the hardest parts of all this, to be completely honest with you. It really is. 

I used to absolutely love—I mean, it was practically my favorite weekend activity—hunting for old clasps. You know, going to estate sales or those big antique fairs out in the county, sifting through boxes of broken vintage jewelry just to find a beautiful, intact Art Deco box clasp with the original paste stones, or maybe a really delicate Victorian barrel clasp. There's just something so thrilling about finding a piece of history like that, rescuing it from a dusty cardboard box, and thinking about how you can incorporate it into a modern design. I could spend hours doing that. And the classes, too. I used to get so much joy out of planning those little jewelry classes I mentioned earlier. I'd sit at my kitchen table with a pot of Earl Grey and draw up all the diagrams, figure out the exact amount of silver clay each student would need, make little sample pendants to show them what we were aiming for... I just loved doing that. 

But lately... I don't know, it's like a switch has been flipped inside me. I'll sit down at my workbench—I have this beautiful vintage oak jeweler's bench with the canvas catch tray underneath—and I'll pull out my organizers, but... I mostly just stare at the trays. I look at all those beautiful clasps I spent so much time hunting down, and the beads, and the wire, and I just feel like none of it is worth starting. It's this overwhelming, heavy feeling of 'why bother?' I'll sit there under the magnifier lamp for maybe twenty minutes, just looking at the little compartments, maybe I'll move a piece of turquoise from one slot to another, and then I just push the tray away. It just feels so utterly pointless right now. It breaks my heart, really, because my work has always been my passion, but the drive to actually create something, to put the pieces together... it's just completely gone.
Was there ever a time when you felt depressed for at least two weeks but did not have the voices, unusual smells, or fears of being watched?

Well, no, not that I can recall... it really didn’t happen like that. Actually, it was quite the opposite, if I'm being honest. When I think back to those worst months, you know, when that heavy, heavy sadness was just pressing down on me so hard that I couldn't even bring myself to care about my bench or my tools... that was exactly when all those other strange things were happening, too. They were all happening at the exact same time. 

I’d be sitting there in the shop, just completely drained, feeling that total loss of interest in everything I usually love, and out of nowhere, I would hear my name being called. Just clear as a bell, echoing right off the glass display cases. And there wouldn't be a soul around. It's such an unsettling feeling, being so low and then having your mind play tricks on you like that.

And the worry... oh, the worry was just eating me alive right alongside the sadness. I was absolutely, one hundred percent sure that the customers coming in weren't there to look at the jewelry at all. I’d see someone lingering by the front window, maybe looking at a display of turquoise pendants I’d put out, and I just knew—I was completely convinced—that they were checking up on our payments. It’s a tough business, retail, especially with precious metals because the overhead is so astronomical. You have to buy all your silver casting grain and your stones up front from the suppliers, so money is always on your mind anyway. 

But this was different. I’d be sitting there, too depressed to even pick up a pair of pliers, hearing my name in an empty room, and absolutely terrified that every person who walked through the door was secretly auditing my finances or making sure I was paying the bills. It was exhausting. So, no, the depression didn't happen by itself without those other things. It was all just... tangled up together into one big, awful mess during those worst months. I couldn't separate the sadness from the voices or the fear if I tried.
When you hear the woman's voice call your name, does it ever say anything about you being worthless or guilty?

Worthless or guilty? Oh, no... no, nothing like that at all. It’s actually quite brief, really. It’s literally just my name. 

I’ll be sitting there at the bench—usually, it happens when the shop is very quiet, you know, like on a Tuesday afternoon when foot traffic is just completely dead and I'm trying to get caught up on my finishing work. I use this Foredom flex shaft tool with these little silicone polishing wheels, and even though the motor has a bit of a hum to it, I'll just hear the voice cut right through it. Just my name, clear as day. 

But it's never cruel or mean. It doesn't tell me I'm a bad person or that I'm failing at the business or anything awful like that. Honestly, the guilt I feel myself about not being productive enough right now, about just staring at my trays and not making anything... well, that's already heavy enough on its own. I certainly do a fine enough job making myself feel guilty, I don't need a voice doing it for me! 

But the voice itself, no. It’s just a woman, sounding almost exactly like a customer who just wandered in from the street and is trying to get my attention from the front display cases while I'm working in the back. Like she's just stepping out of the rain and calling out to see if anyone is minding the store. It’s never full sentences or anything critical or degrading like you’re asking about. It's just... just my name, hanging there in the air, and then when I get up and walk out to the showroom to see who it is, wiping the polishing compound off my hands, there's absolutely no one there. But no, it never says I'm worthless.
Have you ever felt that someone was controlling your thoughts or putting thoughts into your mind?

Controlling my thoughts? Or putting them in my head? Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that. I mean, I know my thoughts are my own, even when they're... well, even when they're a bit jumbled or when that heavy sadness takes over. 

I know some people talk about things like that, feeling like they aren't in control of their own minds, but for me, it's really just... it's just me in here. Sometimes I wish someone else would take over, honestly, especially when I'm sitting at my bench trying to figure out a new setting for a cabochon and I just can't focus. I'll be staring at a piece of silver bezel wire, knowing exactly how I need to measure it and cut it and solder it, but my brain just feels like it's wading through molasses. And then I start thinking about the suppliers and the bills and whether those people looking in the window are checking up on me... but those are definitely my thoughts. My worries. 

No one is forcing them on me or planting them there like seeds. It's just my own mind, running away with itself, or... or just grinding to a complete halt, depending on the day. But it's all me. Just me and the quiet in the shop, and occasionally that voice calling my name, but even then, my thoughts are my own. I've never felt like I was a puppet or anything like that. Just... very tired, and very overwhelmed by my own mind, if that makes sense.
Has this depressed mood lasted for at least two weeks in a row?

Two weeks? Oh, my... it's been much, much longer than that. It feels like it's been stretching on forever, honestly. It's definitely been going on for weeks and weeks in a row without a break. 

Every single day, it's just the same thing. Most mornings, I wake up and there's just this... this flat, heavy sadness sitting right on my chest. It's like the color has completely drained out of the house before I even get out of bed, let alone before I even make it down to the shop. You know how when you wake up and the sun is shining and you think, 'Oh, I'm going to make a pot of coffee and maybe try that new bezel setting technique I saw in that trade magazine'? Well, it's the exact opposite of that. 

I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling fan—it has these little brass accents on the blades that I used to think were so charming when we first moved in, but now they just look dull—and I just feel so incredibly empty and sad. It's a physical weight, I swear it is. And it doesn't lift. It just stays with me while I'm brushing my teeth, while I'm trying to force down a piece of toast, and it follows me all the way to the store. 

I unlock the front door, turn off the alarm, flip on the overhead lights over the display cases, and I just stand there feeling completely hollowed out. It doesn't matter if it's a Monday or a Saturday, the feeling is just constant. So, yes, to answer your question, it has absolutely been at least two weeks. It's just a continuous, unrelenting grayness that I can't seem to shake, no matter how hard I try to push through it.
Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you had the voice, the unusual smells, or the feeling of being watched, but were not depressed at all?

Well... yes, actually. I think there was. It's funny you ask it that way, because I was just thinking about how things were before this awful, heavy feeling took over everything. 

There was a stretch—I want to say it was earlier this spring, before the depression really settled in and made it impossible to get out of bed. I was actually doing quite well! I was still running my Thursday evening wire-wrapping classes for beginners. I had a full roster, eight ladies, and we were making these lovely little copper and turquoise pendants. And I was gardening on the weekends, too. I had just put in a whole new row of hydrangeas along the side of the house... the big mophead kind, you know? The ones that turn blue if you get the soil acidity just right. I was out there with my trowel and my gardening gloves, feeling perfectly fine, not sad at all. Energetic, even.

But during that same time, for several weeks, I was having those other things happen. I'd be in the middle of teaching a class, demonstrating how to use round-nose pliers to make a perfect loop, and I'd hear those noises coming from the polishing room in the back. Not just the voice calling my name, but like... shuffling, or the sound of the flex shaft motor whirring for a second when I knew I had unplugged it. And that feeling of being watched... oh, that was so strong then. I kept worrying that customers—or not even customers, just people out on the sidewalk—were staring through the front window, scrutinizing the business, judging how I was running things, maybe even plotting to break in and steal the silver stock. 

I was so preoccupied with it that I even went and bought a new deadbolt for the back door near the alley. But my mood? My mood was completely fine. I wasn't crying, I wasn't feeling that terrible gray emptiness. I was just... busy, and gardening, and teaching, but constantly looking over my shoulder and hearing things in the back room. So, yes, there was definitely a period of a few weeks where I had all of that going on, but none of the sadness. It's so strange how the mind works, isn't it? Because now it's all just jumbled together with this awful depression.

doctor.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: I came in because when people ask me a simple question, like when a ring repair will be ready, my answer starts going from invoices to garden soil to the mortgage papers and I can see them losing me.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code S021.

patient.answer:
Hi, it's nice to meet you too. Well, I suppose I'm here because of what's been happening at work lately, and it's really starting to bother me. I'm a jeweler, I do a lot of custom metalwork and precious stone settings, repairs, things like that, which I've done for years. But I came in today because I've been having this awful trouble when talking to my customers. 

Someone will come in and ask me a really simple question, like, just asking when a ring repair will be ready for them to pick up. Just a basic, everyday question, right? But when I try to answer them, my answer just starts going all over the place. I'll start talking about the repair invoices, and then somehow that makes me start talking about the garden soil I need to pick up for my flower beds, and before I know it I'm going on about the mortgage papers I was sorting through on my kitchen table the night before. 

I just keep talking and I can actually see them losing me. I can see their expressions change, like they have no idea how we got from a broken clasp to my garden, and honestly, neither do I. It’s just so embarrassing because I know they just want a simple date and time, and I took some college classes in business years ago so I know how to be professional, but I just can't seem to stop my thoughts from stringing all these completely unrelated things together out loud. It just spills out of me before I can catch it.

inference.note: Initial broad differential based on apparent formal thought disorder with derailment/tangentiality. Includes schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis, mood disorder with psychotic features, and possible organic psychotic disorder; insufficient data yet to distinguish.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the disorganized speech is occurring in the context of a manic mood state, which would distinguish mania-related psychosis from schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
doctor.question: Lately, have you been feeling unusually high or euphoric?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about manic symptoms (feeling unusually high or euphoric), which are not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
High? Euphoric? Oh, heavens no. No, I don't think I've felt anything even close to euphoric in... well, I honestly can't even remember. 

I mean, when I hear the word euphoric, I picture someone just bouncing off the walls with joy, you know? Like... like when my sister won a little bit of money on a scratch-off ticket a few years back and she just couldn't stop talking about it. She was so thrilled she took our whole family out to this little Italian place downtown, the one with the really good garlic knots, and she was just glowing the entire night. But me? No, definitely not. I haven't had any sort of burst of happiness or extra energy like that at all. 

If anything, I just wake up, make my coffee—usually just a simple drip, nothing fancy, though sometimes I used to use the French press if I had the time on a Sunday morning... but lately, I just stick to the basic machine because I just want to get it over with. So, no, I'm definitely not feeling high or on top of the world or anything like that. I'm really just trying to get through my workday and figure out why my brain keeps jumbling up my words when I'm standing at the counter with my customers. There's certainly no euphoria in that, let me tell you, it's honestly just incredibly frustrating.

inference.note: No clear euphoria reported, which lowers suspicion for mania, but tangential/disorganized speech can occur in psychotic mania or bipolar disorder, so the differential remains unchanged pending further questioning about psychosis, mood, and medical/substance causes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are hallucinations, which would help distinguish a primary psychotic disorder from mania or other causes.
doctor.question: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: When the shop is quiet I sometimes hear a woman mutter my name from the polishing room or smell burning metal when the torches are off, and it feels real enough that I go check.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I have been hearing voices when no one is there, which corresponds to the symptom of hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, actually. I mean, it's not like a whole crowd of people talking to me or anything like you see in the movies, but... yes. It usually happens when I'm at work and the shop is completely quiet. You know, those lulls in the afternoon, usually around 2:30 or 3:00, when everyone is still at their own jobs and the foot traffic just dies down completely. I'll be sitting there, maybe just sorting through some jump rings or organizing my files, and I'll hear this woman's voice. 

It's always a woman, and she just mutters my name. Just my name, but it sounds like it's coming right out of the polishing room in the back. The first few times it happened, I actually got up and walked back there, thinking maybe someone had slipped through the side door without the bell ringing, or maybe my sister had dropped by to bring me lunch and was trying to surprise me. But there's never anyone there. Just the polishing wheels and the dust collector sitting there turned off. 

And it's not just the voice, either. Sometimes, in that same quiet stretch, I'll suddenly smell burning metal. If you've ever worked with a jeweler's torch, you know exactly that smell—it's very distinct, sharp, almost acidic when the flame hits the flux. I'll smell it so strongly, so clearly, that I'll actually panic for a second. I'll drop whatever I'm doing and run over to the soldering station to make sure I didn't leave a torch on or that a valve isn't leaking. I'll check the dials, I'll check the hoses, I'll even touch the tips of the torches to see if they're warm. But they're always stone cold. Everything is off. But the smell is just so real, and the voice is so real, that I just have to go check every single time, even though part of me knows by now that I'm probably going to find an empty room. It's just so unsettling, you know? To experience something so vividly and then find out it's just... not there.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is an underlying medical or neurologic condition that could explain the hallucinations, to distinguish an organic psychotic disorder from primary psychotic or mood disorders.
doctor.question: Have you had any seizures?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about seizures, which are a general medical condition or neurological symptom, and my symptom profile does not contain any information about experiencing seizures.

patient.answer:
Seizures? Oh, no. No, I've never had a seizure. I mean, I know what they look like, of course. My neighbor, well, my old neighbor from about fifteen years ago, her name was Brenda, she had this little terrier mix that used to have seizures. Poor thing would just fall over in the yard and shake, and Brenda would get so upset, naturally. She'd have to sit there on the grass with him until it passed. But me? No, nothing like that. 

I've always been pretty healthy in that regard. I mean, working with my hands all day, doing such fine, detailed work with the stones and the metal, you really need a steady hand. If I were having seizures, or even just tremors, I don't think I could do my job at all. Setting a tiny diamond into a prong setting takes so much precision, you know? You have to hold the piece just right, apply just the right amount of pressure with the tools. So, no, definitely no seizures. My hands are steady... it's just my thoughts and my words that seem to be getting all tangled up lately. But physically, no, no seizures or anything like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a sustained elevated or irritable mood suggestive of a manic episode, which would distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder or bipolar disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually irritable lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unusual irritability, which is a symptom of mania or hypomania, but it is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Irritable? Well, I wouldn't say I've been unusually irritable, no. I mean, sure, everyone gets a little annoyed now and then, especially when things don't go according to plan. Like last Tuesday, I had this customer come in—a very nice lady, don't get me wrong, she's been coming to me for years—but she brought in this antique filigree ring that her grandmother had given her, and she wanted me to resize it. Now, resizing filigree is always tricky because the metal is so delicate, and if you aren't careful, you can completely ruin the pattern. So I explained all of this to her, very patiently, and told her it would take at least two weeks because I needed to order a specific type of gold solder to match the alloy perfectly. 

But then, not even three days later, she calls the shop wanting to know if it's ready! I had to explain the whole process to her all over again. And yes, in that moment, I suppose I felt a tiny bit of frustration, just because I had been so clear the first time. But I wasn't snapping at her or losing my temper. I kept my voice perfectly level and polite, just like I always do. 

And my sister, she's always telling me I have the patience of a saint, especially with the intricate work I do. You really can't be an irritable person and sit at a bench for six hours straight, peering through a loupe, trying to set a one-millimeter sapphire without scratching the surface. It requires a very calm, very centered disposition. So, no, I don't think I've been feeling unusually irritable. Just the normal, everyday little annoyances, but nothing out of the ordinary, and certainly nothing I can't handle with a deep breath and a cup of tea. It's really just the sadness and the... the confusion with my words and those strange moments in the quiet shop that are bothering me. But my temper? No, that's been perfectly fine.

inference.note: F30.2 removed: patient denies euphoria and irritability, making a manic episode with psychotic symptoms less likely. Ongoing thought derailment plus auditory/olfactory hallucinations still support schizophrenia-spectrum or organic psychosis; bipolar disorder with psychotic symptoms remains possible but less likely than primary psychosis.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are clear depressive episodes, to distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia and bipolar disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most mornings I wake up with this flat, heavy sadness, like the color has drained out of the house before I even get to the shop.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day, which matches the symptom of depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Well, yes... yes, I have. It’s funny you phrase it like that, "most of the day, nearly every day," because that’s exactly what it feels like. It’s this constant, lingering thing. Most mornings I wake up with this flat, heavy sadness, like the color has just completely drained out of the house before I even get out of bed, let alone before I get to the shop. 

It’s hard to explain, really. You know how when you look at a beautiful piece of jewelry, maybe a really nice opal, and it has all that fire and play of color? That’s how life used to feel to me. There were bright spots, things to look forward to, even just small things like a good cup of coffee or a nice chat with a customer. But now, it’s like looking at a piece of rough, unpolished quartz. Just dull and gray. 

I’ll lie there in bed and look at the ceiling, and the thought of getting up and going through the motions just feels so... monumental. I still do it, of course, because I have the shop to run and my sister relies on me to keep things going, but the joy is just gone. I’ll sit at my bench, and even when I’m working on something I used to love, like a really intricate custom setting, I just feel this weight sitting right on my chest. It doesn't go away after lunch, it doesn't go away when I close up the shop for the evening. It’s just this quiet, heavy sadness that follows me around, day in and day out. So, yes, I would say I’ve been feeling depressed almost constantly lately. It’s exhausting, to be honest. Just exhausting to feel so empty all the time.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have occurred outside of depressive episodes, which best distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from major mood disorder with psychotic features and schizophrenia-spectrum conditions.
doctor.question: Have the voice and the burning-metal smell ever happened during a time when you were not feeling depressed?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a stretch before the depression really settled in when I was still running classes and gardening, but for several weeks I kept hearing noises from the polishing room and worrying customers were watching the business.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the psychotic symptoms (hallucinations of voices and smells) occurred during a period without depressive symptoms, which corresponds to Criterion B for Schizoaffective Disorder.

patient.answer:
Well... yes, actually. Yes, they have. It’s strange to think back on it now, because the sadness feels like it’s been here forever, but there was a time before this heavy feeling really settled in. I was actually doing quite well, keeping very busy. I was still running my evening jewelry-making classes at the community center—which I loved doing, teaching people how to solder and work with silver clay, it’s so rewarding to see their faces when they finish their first piece. And I was gardening, too. I have these beautiful heirloom tomatoes I was tending to, and some lovely climbing roses along the trellis in the back. 

But even then, when I was feeling perfectly fine, not depressed at all, I was having these... experiences. It went on for several weeks, I think. I would be in the shop, feeling completely normal, maybe just organizing my tools or sketching a new design, and I kept hearing these noises coming from the polishing room. It sounded like the tumbling machine was running, or like someone was moving the buffs around, but I was the only one there. And the smell of the burning metal would just waft in, so strong I’d have to check the torches even though I hadn't used them all day. 

And during that same time, I started getting so worried that customers were... watching the business. Not just looking in the windows, but really watching. I’d see someone pause outside the shop, maybe admiring a necklace in the display, but I’d get this overwhelming feeling that they were monitoring me, keeping track of my inventory or my hours. I even started keeping the blinds half-drawn during the day, which is terrible for a retail shop, I know, but I just couldn't shake the feeling. So, yes, all of that—the noises, the smells, the worrying—that was happening for weeks while I was still feeling quite energetic and involved with my classes and my garden, long before this terrible sadness took over.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms occurred for weeks outside a mood episode, which argues against mood-congruent psychotic depression and shifts schizoaffective disorder to depressive type (F25.1). Mania remains unsupported, making F25.0 less likely than before; schizophrenia and organic psychosis remain in the differential.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a distinct manic episode, which would support bipolar I disorder with psychotic features over schizoaffective disorder or schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period when you needed much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a decreased need for sleep with high energy, which is a symptom of mania or hypomania. My symptom profile does not include manic symptoms; my sleep disturbance involves insomnia and difficulty settling down, not feeling full of energy on less sleep.

patient.answer:
Less sleep? No, I wouldn't say that. I've always been a fairly consistent sleeper, really. I mean, my sister always jokes that I run like clockwork, and it's true. Usually, I'm in bed by 10:30, maybe 11:00 if I've gotten caught up reading a good book—lately I've been reading this fascinating biography of René Lalique, his glasswork is just incredible, the way he incorporated those natural motifs into the Art Nouveau style, it really makes you think about how we approach design today. But anyway, yes, I'm usually asleep by 11:00 and up by 7:00, because the shop opens at 9:30 and I like to have a good hour and a half to myself in the morning to have my tea, read the paper, and just ease into the day before I have to start dealing with customers and vendors and all of that. 

Even back when I was feeling good, when I was teaching those evening classes and spending all my weekends out in the garden with the tomatoes and the roses, I still needed my full eight hours. I might have been busy and active, but I was definitely tired at the end of the day. In fact, teaching those classes takes a lot out of you, emotionally and physically, hovering over people's shoulders, making sure they don't burn themselves with the micro-torches... by the time I'd get home at 9:00 PM, I'd be ready to just collapse. So, no, I've never had a time where I was just buzzing along on three or four hours of sleep and feeling perfectly fine. If I don't get my rest, my hands get shaky, and you absolutely cannot have shaky hands when you're trying to set a tiny little diamond into a delicate prong setting. It's just not possible. So, no, I've always needed my sleep.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a period of at least two weeks of psychotic symptoms without depression, which best distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from major depression with psychotic features and supports schizophrenia-spectrum illness.
doctor.question: Was there ever a time when the voices or suspicious thoughts lasted for at least two weeks while you were not feeling depressed?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a stretch before the depression really settled in when I was still running classes and gardening, but for several weeks I kept hearing noises from the polishing room and worrying customers were watching the business.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the psychotic symptoms (voices, suspicious thoughts) occurred for a duration of at least two weeks in the absence of depressive symptoms, which corresponds to Criterion B.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, actually, just like I was saying earlier... it's funny how the mind works, isn't it? You kind of lose track of the timeline when you're in the thick of this heavy sadness, but yes, there was definitely a stretch of time before the depression really settled in. I was feeling quite myself, honestly. I was still running my evening classes at the community center, teaching the silver clay and the soldering, which I always found so fulfilling. And I was out in the garden every weekend, tying up those heirloom tomatoes—they get so heavy if you don't support them properly—and tending to the climbing roses. I felt perfectly fine, mood-wise. 

But even then, while I was feeling good, that's when those things started happening, and it went on for several weeks, easily. I would be in the shop, feeling completely normal, maybe sorting through a new batch of semi-precious stones that had just come in from my supplier in Jaipur—they do the most wonderful cuts on their amethysts, really top-notch work—and I'd just keep hearing these noises coming from the polishing room in the back. It was so distinct, like the tumbling machine was running or someone was shuffling the buffs around, but I was entirely alone in the store. 

And that was the exact same time I started getting so incredibly worried that people were watching the business. It wasn't just a fleeting thought, it was this persistent, gnawing worry for weeks. I'd see a customer outside, maybe just looking at the window display, and I'd be absolutely convinced they were monitoring my inventory or keeping track of when I opened and closed. I was so convinced of it that I started keeping the front blinds half-drawn during regular business hours, which my sister told me was ridiculous for a retail shop, but I just couldn't help it. So, yes, all of that—the noises from the back room, the intense worrying about being watched—that all went on for several weeks while I was still gardening and teaching, well before this awful, draining sadness took over my life.

inference.note: Ruled out F31.2: no history of mania/hypomania (no euphoria, decreased need for sleep, or irritability). F06.2 less likely given no seizure history and no evidence provided for a medical/neurologic cause. Persistent psychotic symptoms for several weeks outside depressive episodes supports F25.1 vs F20.0.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has prominent negative symptoms to help distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: Have you found yourself talking much less than usual lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about alogia (decreased speech), which is a negative symptom of schizophrenia not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Talking less? Well... I suppose it might seem like that to some people, but I don't really think so. I mean, my sister called the other day, and we were on the phone for a good forty-five minutes talking about our aunt's estate sale. It's such a complicated situation, trying to divide up all those antique furniture pieces without causing a family rift. Aunt Helen had this gorgeous Victorian settee, beautifully carved mahogany with the original horsehair stuffing, and my cousin Sarah thinks she should have it just because she has a larger living room, which is completely beside the point if you ask me. 

So, no, when I have something to say, or when I'm talking to my sister or my suppliers, I still talk just as much as I ever did. I was just on the phone with my metal supplier yesterday, actually, trying to sort out a mix-up with an order of sterling silver wire. They sent me half-round instead of dead-soft round, and you simply cannot use half-round when you're trying to do delicate wire-wrapping for pendants, it just doesn't sit right against the stones. I had to explain the whole process to the customer service representative, who clearly had no background in jewelry making whatsoever, bless his heart. I must have spent twenty minutes just trying to get him to understand the difference in the gauges and the temper of the metal. 

Now, I will say, because of this heavy, awful sadness I've been feeling, I haven't been going out to social events or chatting up the neighbors over the fence like I used to. When you feel this drained, this utterly exhausted down to your bones, the idea of making small talk about the weather or the local school board elections just feels impossible. It takes so much energy to put on a bright face and pretend everything is fine when inside you just feel like a lead weight. But as far as my actual ability to talk, or how much I speak when I do have a conversation... no, I haven't noticed any change there. I still have plenty to say, it's just that I don't always have the energy to find an audience for it right now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has prominent negative symptoms, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to love hunting for old clasps and planning little jewelry classes, but lately I mostly stare at the trays and feel like none of it is worth starting.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about losing interest in previously enjoyed activities, which maps directly to the Loss_of_Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Lost interest... oh, heavens, yes. That's actually been one of the hardest parts of all this, to be completely honest with you. It really is. 

I used to absolutely love—I mean, it was practically my favorite weekend activity—hunting for old clasps. You know, going to estate sales or those big antique fairs out in the county, sifting through boxes of broken vintage jewelry just to find a beautiful, intact Art Deco box clasp with the original paste stones, or maybe a really delicate Victorian barrel clasp. There's just something so thrilling about finding a piece of history like that, rescuing it from a dusty cardboard box, and thinking about how you can incorporate it into a modern design. I could spend hours doing that. And the classes, too. I used to get so much joy out of planning those little jewelry classes I mentioned earlier. I'd sit at my kitchen table with a pot of Earl Grey and draw up all the diagrams, figure out the exact amount of silver clay each student would need, make little sample pendants to show them what we were aiming for... I just loved doing that. 

But lately... I don't know, it's like a switch has been flipped inside me. I'll sit down at my workbench—I have this beautiful vintage oak jeweler's bench with the canvas catch tray underneath—and I'll pull out my organizers, but... I mostly just stare at the trays. I look at all those beautiful clasps I spent so much time hunting down, and the beads, and the wire, and I just feel like none of it is worth starting. It's this overwhelming, heavy feeling of 'why bother?' I'll sit there under the magnifier lamp for maybe twenty minutes, just looking at the little compartments, maybe I'll move a piece of turquoise from one slot to another, and then I just push the tray away. It just feels so utterly pointless right now. It breaks my heart, really, because my work has always been my passion, but the drive to actually create something, to put the pieces together... it's just completely gone.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been at least two weeks of depressive symptoms without psychotic symptoms to distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Was there ever a time when you felt depressed for at least two weeks but did not have the voices, unusual smells, or fears of being watched?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: During the worst months, the heavy sadness and loss of interest were happening at the same time I was hearing my name in the shop and feeling sure customers were checking up on our payments.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the depressive symptoms ever occurred without the psychotic symptoms (voices, smells, fears). This maps to the requirement assessing whether the psychotic symptoms and the mood episode occur concurrently.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not that I can recall... it really didn’t happen like that. Actually, it was quite the opposite, if I'm being honest. When I think back to those worst months, you know, when that heavy, heavy sadness was just pressing down on me so hard that I couldn't even bring myself to care about my bench or my tools... that was exactly when all those other strange things were happening, too. They were all happening at the exact same time. 

I’d be sitting there in the shop, just completely drained, feeling that total loss of interest in everything I usually love, and out of nowhere, I would hear my name being called. Just clear as a bell, echoing right off the glass display cases. And there wouldn't be a soul around. It's such an unsettling feeling, being so low and then having your mind play tricks on you like that.

And the worry... oh, the worry was just eating me alive right alongside the sadness. I was absolutely, one hundred percent sure that the customers coming in weren't there to look at the jewelry at all. I’d see someone lingering by the front window, maybe looking at a display of turquoise pendants I’d put out, and I just knew—I was completely convinced—that they were checking up on our payments. It’s a tough business, retail, especially with precious metals because the overhead is so astronomical. You have to buy all your silver casting grain and your stones up front from the suppliers, so money is always on your mind anyway. 

But this was different. I’d be sitting there, too depressed to even pick up a pair of pliers, hearing my name in an empty room, and absolutely terrified that every person who walked through the door was secretly auditing my finances or making sure I was paying the bills. It was exhausting. So, no, the depression didn't happen by itself without those other things. It was all just... tangled up together into one big, awful mess during those worst months. I couldn't separate the sadness from the voices or the fear if I tried.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the psychotic symptoms are mood-incongruent, which helps distinguish schizoaffective disorder depressive type from schizophrenia with secondary depression.
doctor.question: When you hear the woman's voice call your name, does it ever say anything about you being worthless or guilty?

patient.answer:
Worthless or guilty? Oh, no... no, nothing like that at all. It’s actually quite brief, really. It’s literally just my name. 

I’ll be sitting there at the bench—usually, it happens when the shop is very quiet, you know, like on a Tuesday afternoon when foot traffic is just completely dead and I'm trying to get caught up on my finishing work. I use this Foredom flex shaft tool with these little silicone polishing wheels, and even though the motor has a bit of a hum to it, I'll just hear the voice cut right through it. Just my name, clear as day. 

But it's never cruel or mean. It doesn't tell me I'm a bad person or that I'm failing at the business or anything awful like that. Honestly, the guilt I feel myself about not being productive enough right now, about just staring at my trays and not making anything... well, that's already heavy enough on its own. I certainly do a fine enough job making myself feel guilty, I don't need a voice doing it for me! 

But the voice itself, no. It’s just a woman, sounding almost exactly like a customer who just wandered in from the street and is trying to get my attention from the front display cases while I'm working in the back. Like she's just stepping out of the rain and calling out to see if anyone is minding the store. It’s never full sentences or anything critical or degrading like you’re asking about. It's just... just my name, hanging there in the air, and then when I get up and walk out to the showroom to see who it is, wiping the polishing compound off my hands, there's absolutely no one there. But no, it never says I'm worthless.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are bizarre/Schneiderian, which would favor schizophrenia (F20.0) over schizoaffective disorder, depressive type (F25.1) less directly than the mood-psychosis timing already established.
doctor.question: Have you ever felt that someone was controlling your thoughts or putting thoughts into your mind?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thought insertion or delusions of control. The patient's symptom profile for delusions (S019) only covers beliefs about customers checking on payments, and does not include thought control or thought insertion.

patient.answer:
Controlling my thoughts? Or putting them in my head? Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that. I mean, I know my thoughts are my own, even when they're... well, even when they're a bit jumbled or when that heavy sadness takes over. 

I know some people talk about things like that, feeling like they aren't in control of their own minds, but for me, it's really just... it's just me in here. Sometimes I wish someone else would take over, honestly, especially when I'm sitting at my bench trying to figure out a new setting for a cabochon and I just can't focus. I'll be staring at a piece of silver bezel wire, knowing exactly how I need to measure it and cut it and solder it, but my brain just feels like it's wading through molasses. And then I start thinking about the suppliers and the bills and whether those people looking in the window are checking up on me... but those are definitely my thoughts. My worries. 

No one is forcing them on me or planting them there like seeds. It's just my own mind, running away with itself, or... or just grinding to a complete halt, depending on the day. But it's all me. Just me and the quiet in the shop, and occasionally that voice calling my name, but even then, my thoughts are my own. I've never felt like I was a puppet or anything like that. Just... very tired, and very overwhelmed by my own mind, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a sustained depressive episode meeting the minimum duration criterion, to help distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Has this depressed mood lasted for at least two weeks in a row?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most mornings I wake up with this flat, heavy sadness, like the color has drained out of the house before I even get to the shop.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration and persistence of the depressed mood to establish if it meets the two-week threshold for a depressive episode, which aligns with the Depressed Mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Two weeks? Oh, my... it's been much, much longer than that. It feels like it's been stretching on forever, honestly. It's definitely been going on for weeks and weeks in a row without a break. 

Every single day, it's just the same thing. Most mornings, I wake up and there's just this... this flat, heavy sadness sitting right on my chest. It's like the color has completely drained out of the house before I even get out of bed, let alone before I even make it down to the shop. You know how when you wake up and the sun is shining and you think, 'Oh, I'm going to make a pot of coffee and maybe try that new bezel setting technique I saw in that trade magazine'? Well, it's the exact opposite of that. 

I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling fan—it has these little brass accents on the blades that I used to think were so charming when we first moved in, but now they just look dull—and I just feel so incredibly empty and sad. It's a physical weight, I swear it is. And it doesn't lift. It just stays with me while I'm brushing my teeth, while I'm trying to force down a piece of toast, and it follows me all the way to the store. 

I unlock the front door, turn off the alarm, flip on the overhead lights over the display cases, and I just stand there feeling completely hollowed out. It doesn't matter if it's a Monday or a Saturday, the feeling is just constant. So, yes, to answer your question, it has absolutely been at least two weeks. It's just a continuous, unrelenting grayness that I can't seem to shake, no matter how hard I try to push through it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a full two-week period of psychotic symptoms without any mood symptoms, which best distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you had the voice, the unusual smells, or the feeling of being watched, but were not depressed at all?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a stretch before the depression really settled in when I was still running classes and gardening, but for several weeks I kept hearing noises from the polishing room and worrying customers were watching the business.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the psychotic symptoms (hallucinations and delusions) ever occurred for a period of at least two weeks without the depressed mood, which directly corresponds to Criterion B for schizoaffective disorder.

patient.answer:
Well... yes, actually. I think there was. It's funny you ask it that way, because I was just thinking about how things were before this awful, heavy feeling took over everything. 

There was a stretch—I want to say it was earlier this spring, before the depression really settled in and made it impossible to get out of bed. I was actually doing quite well! I was still running my Thursday evening wire-wrapping classes for beginners. I had a full roster, eight ladies, and we were making these lovely little copper and turquoise pendants. And I was gardening on the weekends, too. I had just put in a whole new row of hydrangeas along the side of the house... the big mophead kind, you know? The ones that turn blue if you get the soil acidity just right. I was out there with my trowel and my gardening gloves, feeling perfectly fine, not sad at all. Energetic, even.

But during that same time, for several weeks, I was having those other things happen. I'd be in the middle of teaching a class, demonstrating how to use round-nose pliers to make a perfect loop, and I'd hear those noises coming from the polishing room in the back. Not just the voice calling my name, but like... shuffling, or the sound of the flex shaft motor whirring for a second when I knew I had unplugged it. And that feeling of being watched... oh, that was so strong then. I kept worrying that customers—or not even customers, just people out on the sidewalk—were staring through the front window, scrutinizing the business, judging how I was running things, maybe even plotting to break in and steal the silver stock. 

I was so preoccupied with it that I even went and bought a new deadbolt for the back door near the alley. But my mood? My mood was completely fine. I wasn't crying, I wasn't feeling that terrible gray emptiness. I was just... busy, and gardening, and teaching, but constantly looking over my shoulder and hearing things in the back room. So, yes, there was definitely a period of a few weeks where I had all of that going on, but none of the sadness. It's so strange how the mind works, isn't it? Because now it's all just jumbled together with this awful depression.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms occurred for several weeks in the absence of depression, while a major depressive episode is also clearly present and there is no evidence of mania/hypomania. This rules out F20.0 in favor of depressive-type schizoaffective disorder.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a sustained major depressive episode with anhedonia and pervasive low mood lasting well over 2 weeks, together with psychotic symptoms. Crucially, hallucinations and persecutory ideas also occurred for several weeks during a period when the patient was not depressed, which supports schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, rather than major depressive disorder with psychotic symptoms. There is no evidence of manic or hypomanic episodes, and no seizure history to suggest an organic explanation explored in the interview.
